en: The Sūtra of the King of Lapis Lazuli Radiance, the Medicine Guru.
Oṃ, homage to the Omniscient One!
Homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharāja.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, arrived in due course at the great city of Vaiśālī.
He arrived there.
Now, the Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī at the foot of the Vādyasvara tree, together with a great community of monks consisting of eight thousand monks and thirty-six thousand bodhisattvas;

he was surrounded and honored by an assembly of kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and a host of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as he taught the Dharma.
He taught.

Then Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, by the power of the Buddha, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "May the Blessed One teach the names of those Tathāgatas."

"Having heard the detailed exposition of their former vows, we shall purify all karmic obscurations for the sake of benefiting sentient beings in the future time, in the final age, when the semblance of the True Dharma prevails.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"

O Mañjuśrī, you are the one of great compassion. Having generated immeasurable compassion, you cause them to enter meditative concentration for the sake, welfare, and happiness of sentient beings obstructed by various karmic hindrances, and for the benefit of gods and humans.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen; pay close and careful attention, and I shall speak.
"So be it, Blessed One," [he replied].
Thus Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him:
"Mañjuśrī, in the eastern direction, beyond as many buddha-fields from this buddha-field as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers, there is a world-system named Vaidūryanirbhāsā."

There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when that Blessed One Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha was formerly practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, he made these twelve great vows.

What are the twelve great vows? His first great vow was: "When, in a future time, I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then may immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite world-systems be illumined, heated, and made radiant by the light of my body."
And just as I am endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and my body is adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics,
in that very same way may all sentient beings come to be.

His second great vow was this: "When, in a future time, I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, then upon my attainment of awakening, my body shall be utterly pure inside and out like a priceless lapis lazuli gem, endowed with stainless radiance.
My vast body shall be manifest with a corresponding splendor and majesty."
The networks of its rays would surpass even the beams of the sun and moon; and whatever beings are born in this world-system,
as well as those men, should they travel in various directions during the darkness of the night, [they would be illuminated].
Touched by my light in all directions, may they perform virtuous deeds.

His third great vow was this: "When, in the future... at that time, once I have attained awakening, may those beings of the immeasurable realm of sentient beings, through the empowerment of my boundless power of wisdom and skillful means, possess inexhaustible resources for their enjoyment and utilization;
and may no being whatsoever suffer from any deficiency."

His fourth great vow was: "When, in the future... then, having attained awakening, may I establish those beings who have entered upon wrong paths—those who have entered the path of the Śrāvakas and those who have entered the path of the Pratyekabuddhas—in the unsurpassed path of awakening, the Mahāyāna."

His fifth great vow was: "When, in the future—then, once I have attained awakening—whatever beings should practice the holy life under my teaching, may they all possess unbroken morality and be well-restrained;
and may no one [violate it]."
If, having heard my name, one who has failed in moral discipline should go to an evil rebirth anywhere, [may I not attain enlightenment].

His sixth great vow was this: "In the future, when I have attained awakening, may all those beings who are deficient in body, with impaired faculties, of ugly complexion, dull-witted, mute, lame, humpbacked,

leprous, crippled, blind, deaf, insane, or afflicted by whatever other diseases of the body there may be, upon hearing my name, become endowed with all their faculties and possess limbs that are perfectly complete."

His seventh great vow was this: "In the future, when I have attained awakening, may those beings who are afflicted by various diseases, who are without protection, without refuge, deprived of medicines and requisites, helpless, poor, and suffering—
if my name should fall upon their ears, [may they be freed from all ailments]."
May all their diseases be pacified,
and may they be free from illness and free from affliction until the final attainment of enlightenment.

His eighth great vow was: "In the future, whenever any woman— desiring to be liberated from the female state, which is defiled by hundreds of various female faults, and from the womb of the female sex, regarding it with loathing— should bear my name in mind,
may that woman no longer have a female state until she reaches the culmination of enlightenment."

His ninth great vow was this: "When, in the future—having attained awakening at that time—I shall turn back all sentient beings who are bound by the fetters of Māra’s snares and have fallen into the perilous thickets of various views;
having diverted them from all the snares of Māra and the courses of false views, I shall establish them in right view and gradually demonstrate to them the conduct of a bodhisattva."
His tenth great vow was this: "In the future, when I have attained awakening, may all those beings who are terrified by the fear of kings and the like,

or those who are bound in fetters and imprisoned, or those deserving of death, or those afflicted by many calamities and humiliated, or those struck by physical, verbal, and mental sufferings— may they,
upon hearing my name and through the power of my merit, be completely liberated from all fears and afflictions."

His eleventh great vow was this: "When, in the future... then, when I have attained awakening, those beings who are inflamed by the fire of hunger and are intent on the search for food and drink, and who consequently commit evil deeds—if they should hold my name in mind, [may they be relieved]."
I would satisfy their bodies with food endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.

His twelfth great vow was this: "In the future, when I have attained enlightenment, may all those beings who are destitute of clothing, impoverished, and afflicted by cold, heat, gadflies, and mosquitoes,
experiencing suffering day and night— if they should hold my name in mind,"
I would provide them with the enjoyment of clothing,
and I would present them with sensual pleasures dyed in various colors;
and by means of diverse jewel ornaments, perfumes, garlands, ointments, musical instruments, cymbals, and drums, I would fulfill all the intentions of all sentient beings.

Mañjuśrī, these twelve great vows were made by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, while he was formerly practicing the conduct of awakening. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, neither in an eon nor in the remainder of an eon is it possible to exhaustively describe the vow of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, nor his array of qualities of the Buddha-field.

That buddha-field is utterly pure; it is free from stones, pebbles, and gravel; it is devoid of the faults of desire; it is free from the sound of suffering in the lower realms; and it is without women.

That great earth is made of lapis lazuli, and its walls, enclosures, palaces, gateways, windows, lattices, and turrets are composed of the seven precious gems; it is just like the world-system Sukhāvatī.
In that world-system Vaidūryanirbhāsā, there were two bodhisattva mahāsattvas who were the leaders of those immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattva mahāsattvas: one was named Sūryavairocana,
and the second was Candravairocana.
Those who uphold the treasury of the true Dharma of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha—
therefore, Mañjuśrī, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family should make a vow to be reborn in that buddha-field.
Furthermore, the Blessed One addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there are ordinary beings who do not know wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Overcome by greed and lacking understanding, they do not practice giving, nor do they understand the great ripening of the fruit of giving."
Fools and the ignorant, deficient in the faculty of faith, are preoccupied with the momentary accumulation of wealth;
their minds do not incline toward the distribution of gifts.
When the time for giving arrives, they experience mental anguish as if their own bodies were being cut or their own flesh were being torn away.
And there are many beings who do not consume [food] themselves,
let alone give it to their mothers, fathers, wives, or daughters,
much less to their male and female slaves or laborers.
How much more so for other supplicants!
Such beings, having passed away from here, will be reborn in the world of hungry ghosts or in the animal realm.
However, those who, while formerly being human, have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, [shall not fall into such states].

There, for those dwelling in the world of Yama or dwelling in the animal realm, the name of that Tathāgata will become manifest before them. Merely by recollecting it, they will pass away from there and be reborn once again in the human world.
They will also possess the recollection of their past lives.
Frightened by the fear of miserable rebirths, they will no longer seek the qualities of sensual pleasure;
rather, they will delight in giving and speak in praise of generosity.
By means of total renunciation, they will gradually bestow their hands, feet, head, eyes, flesh, and blood upon supplicants,
let alone any other mass of wealth.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are beings who, having undertaken the precepts for the sake of the Tathāgata, fall into a failure of morality,
or occasionally fall into a failure of view or a failure of conduct.
Furthermore, those who have failed in ethical discipline may become possessed of ethical discipline and guard their morality,
yet they do not seek out extensive learning.
Furthermore, they do not understand the profound meaning spoken by the Tathāgata;
moreover, those who are learned will become conceited and stiff with pride.

Devoted to envy toward others, they despise and reject the true Dharma. Such deluded men are partisans of Māra; having themselves entered upon a wrong path, they cause many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other beings to fall into a great abyss.

For such beings as these, for the most part, there will be rebirth in the dwellings of hell. However, among them, those who have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, while remaining in that hell, will— through the power of the Buddha— have that Tathāgata’s name clearly present before them.
Having passed away from there, they will be reborn once more in the world of humans, endowed with right view, energetic, and possessed of virtuous intentions.
Having renounced their homes and gone forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata, they will gradually fulfill the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are beings who speak in praise of themselves while being miserly,

and who utter dispraise of others. These beings, who exalt themselves and disparage others, having treated one another with contempt, will experience suffering in the three lower realms for many thousands of years.
After the passing of many thousands of years, having died from there, they are reborn among the animal wombs such as cattle, horses, camels, and donkeys.
Beaten by the strokes of whips and sticks, their bodies tormented by hunger and thirst, they travel along the road carrying heavy burdens.
If, at some time, they should obtain a human birth,
They will always be reborn in low-born families and will remain under the control of others as slaves.
However, those who, while previously existing as human beings, have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, [shall not suffer such fates].
By that root of merit, they will be completely liberated from all sufferings;
they will possess sharp faculties and be wise, discerning, and intelligent. Devoted to the pursuit of the wholesome, they will constantly obtain the company of spiritual friends.
Having severed the snare of Māra, they shatter the eggshell of ignorance, dry up the river of afflictions,
and are completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, fear, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are beings who delight in slander and cause sentient beings to engage in mutual strife, conflict, and dispute.
With minds intent on mutual conflict, those beings perform various kinds of unwholesome actions through body, speech, and mind;
desiring each other's harm, they constantly strive for one another's misfortune.
They invoke forest deities, tree deities, and mountain deities;
they invoke various spirits in cremation grounds;
and they deprive animals belonging to the animal realm of their lives.
They worship yakṣas and rākṣasas who consume flesh and blood;

having fashioned either the name or a physical image of that enemy, they perform terrible spells there, desiring—by means of the application of *kākhorda* and *vetāla* rites—to bring about an end to life or the destruction of the body.
However, for those who have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha...
It is impossible for anyone to create obstacles for them;
and they all dwell with minds of mutual loving-kindness, minds of benefit, and minds free from malice, content with their respective possessions.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, these four assemblies— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
and whatever other faithful sons of noble family or daughters of noble family observe the fast-endowment (upavāsa) endowed with the eight limbs of the noble ones,
or shall maintain the precepts for one year or for three months;
Those who have such a vow and such an intention— “By this root of merit, may we be reborn in the western direction, in the world-system Sukhāvatī, where the Tathāgata Amitāyus resides”—

and those who shall hear the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, for them at the time of death, eight bodhisattvas will arrive by means of their supernatural power and appear before them.
There they will appear by spontaneous birth upon lotuses of various colors;
some, moreover, will be reborn in the world of the gods.
For those who have been reborn there, their former roots of merit are not exhausted.
And there will be no going to an evil rebirth;
having passed away from there, they will be reborn here in the human world as kings,
universal monarchs (cakravartin) who rule over the four continents.
They will establish many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, others will be reborn in great kṣatriya families, in great brahmin families, and in families abundant with wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses;
they will be endowed with physical beauty.
They will be endowed with sovereign power and they will be endowed with a retinue;
and whatever woman, having heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, shall take it up [in her heart].
For him, that very last state of being female is to be expected.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in the future time, in the final age, I shall cause those faithful sons of good family and daughters of good family to hear the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha;
I shall even bring the name of the Buddha to their ears, at least within the state of sleep."
Those who shall uphold, recite, teach, master, and extensively proclaim this jewel of a sūtra to others, and who shall write it down or cause it to be written down—
Or, having committed it to a book, they shall honor it with various flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, umbrellas, banners, and flags;
it should be wrapped in five-colored cloths and placed in a clean location.
Wherever this sūtra is established, [there it shall remain].
There, the four great kings with their retinues, as well as many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other gods, will approach;
there this sutra shall circulate.
And those, Blessed One, shall proclaim this jewel of a sutra;

and by upholding the name of that Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, as well as the detailed exposition of the distinctions of that Tathāgata’s former special vows, there shall be no untimely death for them.
No one is able to take away their vital energy (*ojas*), and even if their vital energy has been taken away, they recover it once again.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī."
It is even so,
just as you say.
Mañjuśrī, any faithful son of good family or daughter of good family who wishes to perform an offering to that Tathāgata,
He should have an image of that Tathāgata made,
and for seven days and nights he should observe the fast endowed with the noble eightfold path.

Being pure, having prepared pure food, in a pure place— having strewn various flowers, perfumed with various incenses, and adorned with various cloths, parasols, banners, and flags— in that spot of earth, he should [proceed].

With limbs well-bathed, wearing pure and stainless garments, with a mind that is stainless, untroubled, and free from ill-will, one should maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and [a mind of equanimity], being even-minded toward all sentient beings.
While the various musical instruments are played in concert, that image of the Tathāgata should be circumambulated, and the fulfilled vows of that Tathāgata should be brought to mind.
This sutra should be set forth.
Whatever one intends, whatever one aspires for—
It fulfills every aspiration:
if one desires a long life,
one becomes long-lived.
If he prays for enjoyment,
he becomes possessed of abundant enjoyments; if he prays for sovereignty, [he attains it].
One attains that with little difficulty.
If one desires a son,
one obtains a son.
Those who see an evil dream here,
or where a crow is perched as an ill omen,
or where hundreds of inauspicious things are present—
They should perform worship to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha;
then all evil dreams, ill omens, and inauspicious conditions will be pacified.
For those who have fear of water, poison, weapons, heat, fierce elephants, lions, tigers, bears, hyenas, leopards, venomous snakes, scorpions, centipedes, stinging insects, mosquitoes, and so forth—
They should perform worship to that Tathāgata;
they will be completely liberated from all fears,
including those who have fear of thieves and fear of robbers.
With these, one should perform worship for that Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, those faithful sons of noble family or daughters of noble family who take refuge in the Three Jewels for as long as they live,
who do not have other deities,
and who uphold the five precepts;
And those bodhisattvas who maintain the bodhisattva vow consisting of four hundred excellent precepts,
and furthermore, those monks who have gone forth from the household life and maintain two hundred and fifty precepts;

If those bhikṣuṇīs who uphold the five hundred training rules, or those who have fallen away from any one of the training rules as they were undertaken, should be terrified by the fear of miserable rebirths,
they should hold in mind the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.
No further suffering from going to the three lower realms is to be expected for them.
Furthermore, if any woman, at the time of childbirth, experiences intense, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations,
she who should recollect the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, [shall be freed from it].
And one should perform worship;
she will give birth easily and [obtain] a son with all limbs fully complete.
He will give birth to one who is handsome, pleasing, beautiful to behold, with sharp faculties and great intelligence;
he will be healthy and free from much illness, and it will not be possible for non-human beings to steal away his vital energy.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do you have faith and conviction that I shall describe the qualities of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha?
Or do you have any doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation regarding this profound sphere of the Buddhas?"
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, I have no doubt, nor perplexity, nor uncertainty regarding the discourses spoken by the Tathāgata.
For what reason?
Because there is no impurity in the conduct of body, speech, or mind among the Tathāgatas."

Blessed One, even if these two, the moon and the sun, so possessed of great supernatural power and such great majesty, were to fall to the earth, or even if Sumeru, the king of mountains, were to move from its place,
the word of the Buddhas could never be otherwise.
However, Venerable Sir, there are beings who lack the faculty of faith;
having heard of this sphere of the Buddha, they will say: "How can such qualities and benefits arise from merely recollecting the name of that Tathāgata?
They will neither believe nor have conviction in it.
They reject it;
for them, this will lead to misfortune, lack of welfare, lack of happiness, and downfall for a long night.
The Blessed One said: "It is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question."
It is impossible that a sentient being who has heard the name of that Tathāgata should go to a state of woe or an evil rebirth; such a thing cannot occur.
And, Ānanda, the range of the Buddhas is difficult to believe. That you, Ānanda, have faith and conviction in it— this should be seen as the power of the Tathāgata.

This is not the domain of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, with the exception of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are bound to only one more birth. Ānanda, the attainment of human birth is difficult to find;
faith and reverence toward the Three Jewels are difficult to find.
Extremely difficult to encounter is the hearing of the name of the Tathāgata.
Ānanda, the bodhisattva conduct of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, is immeasurable, and his skill in means is also immeasurable.
And his specific expansion of vows is immeasurable.
If I so desired, Ānanda, I could describe in detail and analyze the conduct of that Tathāgata as a bodhisattva for an eon, or for the remainder of an eon;
yet, Ānanda, it would be exhausted in a short time.
But it is not possible to reach the end of the detailed account of the specific former vows of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.
Now at that time, in that very assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Trāṇamukta who was present and seated.
Rising from his seat, draping his upper robe over one shoulder, and placing his right knee upon the ground, he bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable Blessed One, in the future time, in the final age, there will be beings afflicted by various diseases, their limbs wasted away by chronic illness."

With their throats and lips parched by hunger and thirst, facing death and surrounded by weeping friends, kinsmen, and blood-relations, seeing the directions as darkness and being dragged away by the messengers of Yama,
their consciousness— while the body lies upon its bed— is led into the presence of Yama, the King of Dharma.
And whatever wholesome or unwholesome deed has been performed by that person, which is naturally bound to that being, [is then revealed].

Having recorded all of that in writing, it is presented to Yama, the King of Dharma. Then Yama, the King of Dharma, questions him and calculates his wholesome or unwholesome deeds exactly as they were performed, and issues his command accordingly.
In that regard, if those friends, kinsmen, and blood relatives should go for refuge to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, on behalf of that sick person,
and should perform worship to that Tathāgata,
it is possible that his consciousness might return once again.
He perceives himself as if having entered into a dream;
whether on the seventh day, or the twenty-first day,
or the thirty-fifth day, or the forty-ninth day, his consciousness shall return once again.
He would attain mindfulness.
Whether his action was wholesome or unwholesome, the ripening of that karma would become directly evident to him.
Having known this, he would never again commit a sinful or unwholesome deed for the sake of his life.
Therefore, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family should perform worship to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the bodhisattva named Trāṇamukta: "Noble son, how should worship be performed for that Blessed One, Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha?

The bodhisattva Trāṇamukta replied: "Venerable Ānanda, those who wish to liberate someone from a great illness should, for the sake of that sick person, observe the fast endowed with the eight noble limbs for seven days."
One should perform worship and service for the community of monks with food, drink, and all necessary requisites according to one's ability.
One should bring to mind the name of the Blessed One, Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, three times during the night and three times during the day.
This sutra should be recited forty-nine times.
Forty-nine lamps should be lit.
Seven images should be made.
For each image, seven lamps should be lit.
Each individual lamp should be made the size of a cartwheel.
If the light does not diminish on the thirty-ninth day,
it should be understood that all prosperity is attained.
Fifty-nine five-colored banners should be made.
Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda, for those anointed Kṣatriya kings who may be confronted by calamities or misfortunes—

whether it be the affliction of disease, the oppression of their own army, the oppression of a foreign army, the oppression of the stars, the oppression of lunar or solar eclipses, the oppression of unseasonable winds and rain, or the oppression of drought;
or if inauspicious signs, contagious diseases, or disasters have arisen—
That anointed Kṣatriya king should maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and should release those beings who have fallen into bondage;
furthermore, he should perform for that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, the offerings as previously described.
Then, by this root of merit of that consecrated Kṣatriya king, and through the detailed account of the particular former vows of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha,
there will be security in that realm and an abundance of food;
there will be timely winds, rains, and a bountiful harvest.
And all the beings dwelling in that realm were free from illness, happy, and full of great joy;
nor did wicked yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, or piśācas harass the beings in that realm,
and they saw no ill omens whatsoever.
And for that consecrated Kṣatriya king, there will be an increase in lifespan, complexion, strength, health, and sovereignty.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta: "Noble son, how does one whose lifespan is exhausted increase it once again?
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta replied: "Venerable Ānanda, have you not heard from the Tathāgata that there are untimely deaths?"
In order to counteract those [conditions], the application of mantras and medicinal herbs has been taught.
There are beings who are afflicted by disease,
yet their illness is not severe, though they lack medicine and an attendant.
Or if physicians administer medicine;
this is the first untimely death.
The second untimely death is when one meets their end through royal punishment.
The third untimely death is that of those who are excessively heedless and live in negligence; their vital energy (*ojas*) is snatched away by humans.
The fourth untimely death is that of those who pass away by being consumed by fire.
The fifth untimely death is that of those who die by water. The sixth untimely death is that of those who dwell among lions, tigers, serpents, and fierce wild beasts, and die there.
The seventh untimely death is for those who fall from a mountain precipice.

The eighth untimely death is for those who die through the application of poisons, *kākhorda* spells, or *vetāla* rites. The ninth untimely death is for those who, afflicted by hunger and thirst, pass away in distress while unable to obtain food or drink.
These premature deaths have been briefly described by the Tathāgata;
there are, moreover, immeasurable other types of premature death.
Then, indeed, twelve great yakṣa generals were assembled there in that assembly, namely: the great yakṣa general named Kiṃbhīra, the great yakṣa general named Vajra,
and the great yakṣa general named Mekhila.
The great yakṣa general named Anila, the great yakṣa general named Anila, and the great yakṣa general named Saṇṭhila.
The great yakṣa general named Indala,
the great yakṣa general named Pāyila, and the great yakṣa general named Mahāla.
The great yakṣa general named Cidāla,
the great yakṣa general named Caundhula, and the great yakṣa general named Vikala.

These twelve great yakṣa generals, each surrounded by their own retinues of followers, spoke thus with one voice to the Blessed One: "We have heard, through the power of the Buddha and by the grace of the Blessed One, the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha. Henceforth, we shall have no fear of the miserable states of existence."
We, united and in harmony, for as long as life lasts, go for refuge to the Buddha, go for refuge to the Dharma, and go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
We shall exert ourselves for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings. Specifically, whoever shall propagate this sutra in a village, a city, a district, or a forest hermitage,
or whoever shall uphold the name of that Blessed One, Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, [for them we shall act].
As long as he performs worship and service, we shall protect that being and preserve him.
"We shall liberate them from all inauspiciousness and we shall fulfill the hopes of them all.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to those yakṣa generals, saying: "Excellent, excellent, great yakṣa generals!"
Since you, recollecting your gratitude toward that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, have set out for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma discourse? And how should I remember it?
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Ānanda, remember this Dharma discourse as 'The Detailed Account of the Special Former Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha'."
Remember this as "The Vow of the Twelve Great Yakṣa Generals."
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and the Venerable Ānanda were uplifted in mind.
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta,
those Bodhisattvas,
and those Great Śrāvakas.
And those kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders,
the entire assembly,
and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra entitled *Āryabhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharāja*.
